title: Superposition and 'no definite value' are interpretation-dependent
summary: The claim that a quantum system genuinely has no definite value before measurement is one reading, not a shared fact.
body: The v1 article said a system in superposition genuinely has no definite value until measured, and that this is not ignorance. That is a common textbook reading associated with Copenhagen-style views. It is not agreed by every interpretation that uses the same mathematics. The Stanford Encyclopedia entries on Bohmian mechanics (Sheldon Goldstein) and on many-worlds (Lev Vaidman) describe live alternatives: one assigns definite positions guided by the wave function, and one treats the wave function as describing branching outcomes rather than a collapse to a single value. The formalism's empirical predictions are much better settled than the metaphysics. This is allowed to remain not settled.
said_by: disputed; see Goldstein, Vaidman, Hilgevoord and Uffink

contested_views.label: Textbook / Copenhagen-style reading
contested_views.summary: A measurement outcome is not a pre-existing value merely revealed. The v1 article states this reading as fact.

contested_views.label: Bohmian mechanics
contested_views.summary: Particles have definite positions at all times; the wave function guides them. Goldstein's SEP entry is a statement of this view.

contested_views.label: Many-worlds
contested_views.summary: The universal wave function does not collapse; apparent definiteness is branching. Vaidman's SEP entry is a statement of this view.
